title: Exchange and ventilation: two linked jobs
subtitle: Move air, maintain a gradient and explain diffusion
objective: Explain how ventilation and alveolar structure support gas exchange, using an idealised comparison model.

sow.alignment: C33 improved revisit of earlier diffusion/lung lessons, linked to Pearson 8.2–8.5B. Fick’s-law reasoning is Biology-specific content, not labelled Higher-only. The core connects ventilation, gradients and short diffusion distance; no human breathing practical is required.

priorLearning: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient.
Blood circulates between lungs and tissues.
A rate describes change per unit time.
success: Distinguish ventilation from diffusion and cellular respiration.
Explain thin, moist, large-area alveoli and blood flow using a mechanism.
Predict the effect of changing one diffusion factor while holding others constant.

vocabulary.meaning: Movement of air into and out of the lungs.
A small air sac in the lungs where gases exchange with capillary blood.
A difference in concentration across a distance.
The distance particles must cross during exchange.
A muscular sheet that changes thoracic volume during breathing.
A model number for comparing rates; it is not a calibrated measurement of a person.

equipment: Shared evidence sheet, one selected response route, pen and ruler.
Projector or offline HTML/PowerPoint; calculator where useful.
preparation: Print the shared page, one selected response route and the exit page. Routes are alternatives, not extra tasks.
Read the worked answers and note any constructed data before teaching.
safety: Paper and screen lesson; no human sampling, exercise test, breath holding, medicine handling or personal health disclosure.
practicalAlternative: All evidence is supplied. Use paper diagrams and cards, pointing, annotation or dictation if a device is unavailable.

misconceptions.claim: Breathing, gas exchange and respiration are the same process.
misconceptions.correction: Ventilation moves air; diffusion exchanges gases; cellular respiration releases energy in cells.
misconceptions.check: Ask where each process occurs and what changes.

misconceptions.claim: The lungs pump oxygen directly into every body cell.
misconceptions.correction: Air enters by ventilation; oxygen diffuses into blood, which transports it towards tissues.
misconceptions.check: Trace the separate air, exchange and blood stages.

misconceptions.claim: A thicker barrier helps gases cross faster.
misconceptions.correction: With other factors held constant, a longer diffusion distance reduces rate.

misconceptions.claim: A relative model index is a real clinical gas reading.
misconceptions.correction: It compares a specified model and has no clinical calibration.
misconceptions.check: Ask what the index leaves out.

access.supported: Same core concepts with chunked prompts and read-aloud access. Record support used; a pathway is not a diagnosis or fixed attainment label.
access.standard: Explain the supplied evidence independently using accurate scientific terms and units.
access.stretch: Optional deeper transfer or evaluation. Higher-tier-only material is labelled explicitly and is not required for the core outcome.
access.regulation: Offer solo or partner work, a quiet response, a pass and brief reset with clear re-entry. No forced disclosure or public performance.

slides.title: The air moved. Has exchange happened yet?
body: Mission: separate air movement from particle movement.
Then connect both to blood transport.
slides.notes: Invite pupils to distinguish opening a door from people moving through it as a limited analogy; return immediately to actual gas mechanisms.

slides.title: What drives diffusion?
body: R1. In which direction is net diffusion?
R2. What does circulating blood transport from the lungs?
R3. Is respiration simply another word for breathing?
slides.notes: R1: down a concentration gradient. R2: oxygen, with other transported substances. R3: no; cellular respiration releases energy in cells.

slides.title: Follow one gas at a time
body: Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into blood.
Carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into alveolar air.
Each gas follows its own gradient.
slides.notes: Think aloud along oxygen arrow, then carbon-dioxide arrow. State that gases cross the thin exchange surface by diffusion; blood and ventilation maintain differences. Do not claim all blood always has one uniform gas concentration.

visual.title: Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse in opposite directions
visual.description: Simplified alveolar exchange: oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into arriving oxygen-poor capillary blood; carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into alveolar air. A thin barrier separates air and blood. Directions are based on gradients, not active pumping of gases.

slides.title: Air moves because pressure changes
body: Inhalation increases thoracic volume and lowers pressure.
Quiet exhalation reverses the volume change.
slides.notes: Model diaphragm contraction/flattening plus ribs up/out. Pressure falls below surrounding air pressure, so air enters. Quiet exhalation follows relaxation and elastic recoil; forced exhalation is beyond this core model.

visual.title: Ventilation changes volume and pressure
visual.description: Two-panel schematic of quiet breathing. Inhalation: diaphragm contracts/flattens, ribs move up/out, thoracic volume rises and pressure falls below atmospheric pressure so air enters. Quiet exhalation: muscles relax and elastic recoil reduces volume, raising pressure so air leaves.

elements.text:
Diaphragm contracts/flattens
Volume rises; pressure falls
Air enters

Diaphragm relaxes; recoil
Volume falls; pressure rises
Air leaves

slides.title: Explain the exchange adaptations
body: Large area offers more exchange surface.
A thin barrier gives a short diffusion distance.
Ventilation and flow help sustain gradients.
slides.notes: Use the constructed model to illustrate one factor at a time. P→Q doubles area with other model factors equal; P→R doubles thickness. A relative index is not an oxygen saturation, clinical reading or empirical result.

visual.title: Constructed model: compare one factor
visual.description: Idealised relative diffusion-rate indices calculated as area×concentration difference÷thickness with the same omitted proportionality constant. P:2×4/1=8; Q:4×4/1=16; R:2×4/2=4. This is a mathematical comparison, not measured physiological data.

elements.text: Relative model rate index; not a clinical unit

slides.title: Diffusion design desk
body: W1. Which pair changes area only? Predict the faster case.
W2. Which pair changes thickness only? Predict the slower case.
slides.notes: P/Q changes area only: Q is faster in the model. P/R changes thickness only: R is slower. Ask pupils to identify the unchanged columns before giving a conclusion.

table.caption: Constructed idealised comparison; rate index = area × concentration difference ÷ thickness.

slides.title: Trace a ventilation failure in the model
body: W3. Fresh air stops being replaced while exchange continues.
Why may the oxygen gradient decrease?
slides.notes: Alveolar oxygen is removed into blood and not replenished as effectively; the difference can shrink, reducing net oxygen diffusion if other factors are comparable. This is a conceptual case; pupils do not hold their breath.

slides.title: Repair a three-process caption
body: “The diaphragm respires oxygen into the blood.”
Replace it with ventilation, diffusion and respiration in the right places.
slides.notes: Diaphragm action supports ventilation; oxygen diffuses across alveoli into blood; cells use oxygen in aerobic respiration. No process has to be personified.
slides.reveal: Ventilation moves air. Diffusion exchanges gases. Cellular respiration releases energy in cells.

slides.title: Which explanation names the mechanism?
body: Choose the supported claim.
slides.notes: First option correct. Use the two-panel diagrams to separate air movement from gas diffusion.

options.text: A thin exchange barrier helps because it shortens diffusion distance.
options.feedback: Yes, with other factors equal, a shorter path supports faster diffusion.

options.text: The diaphragm directly pushes oxygen through blood-cell membranes.
options.feedback: It changes thoracic volume/pressure; gas exchange across the lung barrier is diffusion.

options.text: A large surface always guarantees fast exchange, regardless of every other factor.
options.feedback: Gradient and distance also matter; one favourable factor is not a universal guarantee.

slides.title: Build an exchange explanation
body: Choose your route.
Use labelled arrows, the comparison table and a model limit.
slides.notes: Core focuses on mechanisms and fair factor comparisons. The formula extension is Biology-specific reasoning, not inherently Higher-only.

slides.title: Make the link from structure to function
body: Structure → effect on exchange → reason.
Separate model predictions from measurements.
slides.notes: Supported S1–S4; standard M1–M4; stretch T1–T4. Check the pressure direction before asking for extended prose.

slides.title: Audience asks: what actually moves?
body: L1. Share one explanation.
Audience asks whether it concerns air, gas particles or blood.
slides.notes: Pupil improves a process label or identifies a relevant gradient. Quiet teacher/TA audience is valid.

slides.title: Use three precise verbs
body: Ventilate air. Diffuse gases. Transport blood.
Then explain cellular respiration separately.
slides.notes: Accept accurate wording rather than these exact verbs. Ask pupil to correct one misleading “pumps oxygen into cells” claim.

slides.title: Three mechanism checks
body: E1. What happens to pressure during inhalation?
E2. Why does a thin barrier help diffusion?
E3. Name one process distinct from respiration.
slides.notes: E1: falls below atmospheric pressure as volume rises. E2: shorter path. E3: ventilation/diffusion. No breathing exercise is requested.

slides.title: Next useful step
body: Pressure • gas gradient • diffusion distance • model scope.
slides.notes: Shared exit minute; use an annotated diagram if writing demand is a barrier.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence | Idealised exchange comparison
pupilPages.intro: All values are relative model inputs, not measured human data. Hold the omitted proportionality constant the same.

blocks.text: Model rule: relative rate index=area×concentration difference÷thickness. It compares directions and ratios; it has no calibrated physiological unit.

cards.title: Air movement case
cards.text: During quiet inhalation, diaphragm contraction and rib movement increase thoracic volume. Compare pressure inside with surrounding air.

cards.title: Gradient case
cards.text: Oxygen is moving from alveolar air into arriving blood. In this scenario, fresh air replacement is reduced while exchange continues.

blocks.prompt: W1. Area-only pair and prediction. W2. Thickness-only pair and prediction. W3. Explain the fresh-air effect.

pupilPages.title: Supported route | Connect the three jobs
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: ventilation; diffusion; blood transport; respiration; gradient; distance.

blocks.prompt: S1. Draw oxygen and carbon-dioxide arrows across an alveolar surface. Label air and blood.
S2. Explain how diaphragm contraction can make air enter during inhalation.
S3. Compare P/Q and P/R. Name the changed factor and predict the faster/slower model case.
S4. Explain one alveolar adaptation and distinguish ventilation from cellular respiration.

pupilPages.title: Standard route | Structure explains exchange
pupilPages.intro: Use causal links rather than listing features alone.

blocks.prompt: M1. Explain the roles of ventilation and blood flow in maintaining gas gradients.
M2. Explain how large area and a thin, moist barrier support gas exchange.
M3. Describe quiet inhalation and exhalation using muscles, volume, pressure and air direction.
M4. Use the table to justify two one-factor comparisons and state why its indices are not clinical readings.

pupilPages.title: Stretch route | Quantify a model carefully
pupilPages.intro: Optional Biology-specific calculation; Fick-style reasoning is not labelled Higher-only. Use the supplied model rule.

blocks.prompt: T1. Calculate relative indices for P, Q and R. Compare Q with P and R with P using ratios.
T2. A new case doubles area and doubles thickness, with the same concentration difference. Predict its rate index relative to the original and explain.
T3. A cube of side 1 unit has area 6 and volume 1; a cube of side 2 units has area 24 and volume 8. Calculate both surface-area:volume ratios and explain one implication for exchange.
T4. State two limitations of using this idealised model to explain a real lung.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection | Say how and why

blocks.prompt: E1. What happens to thoracic pressure during inhalation, and why does air enter?
E2. Why can a thin exchange barrier increase diffusion rate?
E3. Distinguish ventilation or gas diffusion from cellular respiration.
L1. What did your audience ask? Record one stronger mechanism explanation.

answers.label: Retrieval and We do
answers.answer: R1: down a concentration gradient; R2: oxygen; R3: respiration differs from breathing. W1: P/Q changes area only; Q has twice the index. W2: P/R changes thickness only; R has half the index. W3: less fresh-air replacement can reduce alveolar oxygen and the oxygen gradient as exchange continues.

answers.label: Caption repair and hinge
answers.answer: Ventilation moves air because volume/pressure changes. Oxygen diffuses into blood across alveoli. Cellular respiration releases energy in cells. Correct hinge: thin barrier shortens diffusion distance; diaphragm does not directly force oxygen across membranes.

answers.label: S1 / M1
answers.answer: Oxygen arrow air→blood; carbon dioxide arrow blood→air under the stated gradients. Ventilation replenishes air and removes carbon dioxide; blood flow brings relatively oxygen-poor blood and carries exchanged gases away, helping maintain differences.

answers.label: S2 / M3
answers.answer: During inhalation diaphragm contracts/flattens and external intercostals raise ribs up/out; thoracic volume rises, pressure falls below atmospheric and air enters. Quiet exhalation involves relaxation and elastic recoil, reducing volume and raising pressure so air leaves.

answers.label: S3 / M4
answers.answer: P/Q differs only in area: Q faster. P/R differs only in thickness: R slower. Inputs are relative and idealised, so no clinical concentration, saturation or measured exchange rate can be read from the index.

answers.label: S4 / M2
answers.answer: Large total area supports more simultaneous exchange; a thin alveolar/capillary barrier shortens the diffusion path; moisture enables gases to dissolve. Gradients and blood/air replacement are also important. Cellular respiration is an energy-releasing process in cells, not air movement.

answers.label: T1
answers.answer: P = 2 × 4 / 1 = 8; Q = 4 × 4 / 1 = 16; R = 2 × 4 / 2 = 4. Q/P = 2; R/P = 0.5. The numerator uses concentration difference; these are relative indices with the same proportionality constant.

answers.label: T2
answers.answer: Unchanged: twice the area divided by twice the thickness gives the original index if the concentration difference and other model assumptions match.

answers.label: T3
answers.answer: Small cube 6:1; larger cube 24:8=3:1. The larger cube has less surface per unit volume; increasing size can make diffusion-only exchange less adequate for its volume, depending on shape and demand.

answers.label: T4
answers.answer: Idealised uniform barrier/gradient, no real units or diffusion coefficient, no changing blood flow/ventilation, no heterogeneous alveoli or individual physiology. Any two specific limits are valid.

answers.label: Exit and assessment
answers.answer: E1: pressure falls as volume increases, so air moves in from higher external pressure. E2: shorter diffusion distance. E3: accurate ventilation/diffusion versus respiration distinction. Secure core requires a mechanism, not a feature list; reteach with one gas arrow and one pressure arrow.

teacherNotes: 40-minute lesson. Zero-minute slides share the preceding stage allocation.
Choose one response route. Accept accurate speech, pointing with explanation, annotations or writing; record the support used.
A teacher or TA can be a quiet audience: ask one evidence question, then let the pupil revise or justify a decision.
No pupil breath holding, forced breathing, lung-capacity testing or exercise is needed. The entire lesson uses models and supplied evidence.
Fick’s-law factors and the optional relative-index calculation are Biology-specific in this specification; do not label them automatically Higher-tier.
Interactive and paper W1–W3 use identical model inputs. The animated arrows represent direction, not actual particle counts or an individual’s gas exchange.
